stories.headline: Amazon cargo plane overruns Miami runway and kills at least five
stories.dek: The Boeing 767 hit several vehicles after landing in Miami, shut the airport for hours, and left investigators sorting out who died on board or on the ground.
paragraphs: An Amazon cargo plane operated by 21 Air overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, hit several vehicles, and came to rest in a field. At least five people were killed and five were injured. The FAA and NTSB are now investigating the crash.

The aircraft was a Boeing 767-300 flying from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Fire crews found the plane burning and sending up heavy smoke, with an active fuel leak nearby. The airport halted flights for about three hours, then reopened two runways, but delays continued into Sunday night.

Officials have not said whether the dead were on the plane or on the ground, and they have not identified any victims. The condition of the pilot and co-pilot has not been released. Investigators still need to determine why the aircraft failed to stop on the runway.
stories.changes: Travelers using Miami should expect delays and cancellations while investigators and airport crews work at the crash site.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean cargo flying as a whole has become unsafe, and investigators have not yet said what caused this crash.

cover.title: Amazon cargo plane crashes after runway overrun at Miami airport
cover.standfirst: An Amazon cargo plane operated by 21 Air overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, hit several vehicles, and killed at least five people. Five others were injured, three critically. Federal investigators are now examining the Boeing 767 crash while flight delays continue.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: A field of engraved runway centerline dashes runs straight down the page in strict rhythm, seen from above and slightly oblique, with the lower third left mostly bare tarmac for type. One dash in the lower half suddenly fails: it kinks, widens, and becomes the Amazon 767 itself, skidding sideways off the centerline into scrub, trailing black smoke, with two tiny airport service vehicles veering away from its path and a broken perimeter edge at the runway’s end making the overrun unmistakable.
art.note: Quiet, severe, smoke-gray and foam-white with muted orange firelight
art.second_beat: First you see the mechanical repetition of runway markings; then one mark breaks rank and reveals itself as the crashed jet, so the system’s order literally turns into disaster.

stories.headline: Israeli strikes in Lebanon kill nine as fighting grows
stories.dek: Israel increased attacks on Hezbollah after taking a ridge near the border, raising fears it may keep troops on Lebanese land longer.
paragraphs: Israeli strikes in Lebanon killed nine people as bombardment intensified after Israel captured a strategic ridge last week. Israel says it is targeting Hezbollah. The sharper attacks have raised concern in Lebanon and beyond that the fighting may widen and that Israeli forces may stay longer in Lebanese territory.

Hezbollah is the armed Lebanese group backed by Iran that has fought Israel for years across the border. The current fighting has centered on villages, hills and roads in southern Lebanon. Control of high ground matters because it can help direct fire, watch troop movements and hold nearby border areas.

It is still unclear how long Israel plans to hold the ridge or whether the heavier strikes will lead to a broader ground campaign. The full toll from the latest attacks is not yet known. Diplomatic efforts to reduce the fighting face pressure as civilians near the border remain at risk.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means the Israel-Lebanon border is becoming more dangerous and the risk of a longer conflict has grown.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean a full regional war is certain or that the border fighting cannot still be contained.

cover.title: Israeli strikes kill nine in Lebanon as attacks intensify
cover.standfirst: Israeli strikes in Lebanon killed nine people as Israel stepped up attacks on Hezbollah after taking a strategic ridge last week. The fighting is centered near the border. The next question is whether Israel keeps holding Lebanese territory and whether the clashes spread.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: Show the familiar blue border barrels of the UN line in southern Lebanon as a single-file chain physically walking uphill away from the frontier, receding diagonally into Lebanese terrain. Keep the scene stripped down: pale ground, one steep black ridge, and the barrels mid-step with one near the front pitching forward, so it is unmistakably the border marker itself retreating inland as the fighting advances; leave the lower third largely empty for type.
art.note: Grave and stark, with ash gray, smoke black, and a hard red-orange flare.
art.second_beat: At first it’s an absurd procession of barrels; a beat later you realise the border itself seems to be backing away, turning territorial pressure into a visible act.

stories.headline: Delhi student hostel collapse kills at least seven as rescue continues
stories.dek: Rescuers worked through narrow lanes and rain after a five-storey hostel near Delhi University fell in seconds on Sunday afternoon.
paragraphs: A five-storey student hostel collapsed in Delhi's Satya Niketan area on Sunday, killing at least seven people and injuring others. Rescue teams were still searching on Monday because officials said dozens might remain trapped. The building stood near Delhi University housing used by students in private paying guest rooms.

Police said the building may have held as many as 75 beds. It was 40 to 50 years old, and reports said basement work may have been under way to add capacity. Satya Niketan is packed with student hostels, narrow lanes and overhead wires, which slowed heavy rescue equipment.

The number still under the rubble remains unclear, with estimates ranging from several people to 30 or more. Investigators are examining possible illegal construction, renovation work and structural weakening from waterlogging. Delhi's chief minister has ordered an inquiry, and police have named the building owner in a preliminary case.
stories.changes: Students and families in Delhi's hostel districts may face stricter checks on old private buildings and illegal extra floors.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all Delhi student housing is unsafe, but it does expose serious risks in some poorly regulated buildings.

cover.title: Student hostel collapse in Delhi kills at least seven
cover.standfirst: A five-storey private hostel in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University's south campus, collapsed on Sunday afternoon. At least seven people died and more were rescued, while crews searched through the night for others feared trapped under concrete in the crowded student neighborhood.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: In a rain-slashed Satya Niketan lane, seen close and low, two rescuers’ gloved hands and forearms heave up the broken edge of a concrete slab while grit, wires and small fragments shear downward from it. The white space opening beneath the slab is the clean silhouette of a hostel bunk bed—thin frame, ladder, two mattresses—so the absent room appears only as a void being uncovered; keep the lower third mostly quiet as pale floodwater and wet lane surface for type, with the action compressed into the upper two-thirds.
art.note: Quiet, grave, dusty greys and muted brown with one restrained rescue-orange accent.
art.second_beat: First you see the strain of rescue in a cramped lane; a beat later the space under the slab resolves into the bunk bed, turning absence itself into the trapped hostel room.

stories.headline: AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt vote with record 43.8 percent
stories.dek: The far-right party posted its best result in any German state, but fell short of an outright majority.
paragraphs: Alternative for Germany won the Saxony-Anhalt state election with 43.8% of the vote, according to preliminary official results. The result is the party's strongest ever in any German state. Voting took place Sunday, with turnout reaching 77.8%, the highest in the state since German reunification.

Saxony-Anhalt is a state in eastern Germany with about 1.7 million eligible voters. Germany's mainstream parties have long refused to govern with AfD, which is a far-right party. The CDU came second with 17.2%, followed by the SPD on 9.3%, the Greens on 8.9%, the Left on 8.6%, and BSW on 5.3%.

The main question now is who can form a government. AfD did not win an absolute majority, so it needs a partner. BSW said it is open to talks, while other parties reject cooperation with AfD. The CDU also rules out working with the Left, which narrows the options sharply.
stories.changes: For German readers, this raises the chance of the first state government led by AfD and may affect debate before other regional votes.
stories.unchanged: It does not change Germany's federal government today, and no new state coalition has been agreed yet.

cover.title: AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election with 43.8 percent of the vote
cover.standfirst: Alternative for Germany won the Saxony-Anhalt state election on Sunday with 43.8%, its best result in any German state. The CDU fell to 17.2%, and turnout hit 77.8%. AfD fell short of a majority, so coalition talks will decide whether it can lead a state government for the first time.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: A storm of identical ballot slips, all in CDU/federal blue, falls diagonally across an off-white page into a huge simplified ballot box built from one heavy dark-blue shape. Exactly one fluorescent-pink ballot catches on the slot at the lip of the box, bent and stuck half-in, half-out, while all the blue ballots vanish cleanly inside; keep the lower third quiet with only the base of the box and a few fallen slips. No labels, no extra symbols, no people — just the mass of votes and the one obstructed pink ballot at the threshold.
art.note: Tense, civic mood; muted reds, black, cream, and dull blue.
art.second_beat: First read: one result breaks the pattern; second beat: the winner is the only ballot that cannot actually enter power.

stories.headline: Hackers move $320 million in bitcoin from Liquid sidechain
stories.dek: The people behind the transfer say they are white-hat hackers and are exchanging signed messages with Blockstream through Bitcoin transactions.
paragraphs: About $320 million in bitcoin was withdrawn from Liquid, a Bitcoin sidechain run by Blockstream, according to crypto news reports published in the past hour. The people behind the transfer say they are white-hat hackers. They are now communicating with Blockstream through PGP-signed messages embedded in Bitcoin transactions.

Liquid is a separate network linked to Bitcoin and used to move tokenized bitcoin and other assets more quickly between participants. A white-hat hacker claims to find a security flaw to expose it, not to keep the money. PGP signatures are a way to prove a message really came from a specific cryptographic key.

It is still unclear whether this was an authorized security intervention, a theft presented as one, or a negotiation after a breach. The reports do not yet show whether funds are safe, frozen, or recoverable. Blockstream's own account, the technical flaw, and any timetable for return remain unresolved.
stories.changes: If you hold assets on a crypto platform, this is a reminder that network bridges and sidechains can add risks beyond Bitcoin itself.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the Bitcoin network was hacked, and it does not by itself show that every bitcoin holder is affected.

cover.title: Hackers withdraw $320 million in bitcoin from Liquid network
cover.standfirst: Reports say about $320 million in bitcoin was moved out of Blockstream's Liquid sidechain within the past hour. The people behind it call themselves white-hat hackers and are sending PGP-signed messages through Bitcoin transactions. It is not yet clear whether the money will be returned or how the access was gained.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On warm off-white seamless, photograph a thick braided steel security cable lock as the only object, entering from the upper left and trailing diagonally toward center so the lower third stays mostly clear. The lock’s cut end has come apart impossibly: instead of wire, it is spilling a tight stream of gold bitcoin-style coins from inside its own body, with a few coins already scattered and one or two still mid-roll, as if the secured system itself has turned into the source of the theft. Keep it deadpan, crisp, and physical — no labels, no extra props, no visible cutting tool, just the lock misbehaving.
art.note: Cold, forensic mood; charcoal, steel blue, and pale screen light.
art.second_beat: First read: security breach; second beat: the thing meant to secure the assets is literally what is leaking them.

stories.headline: Rocket reaches orbit from mainland Europe for the first time
stories.dek: A small launcher flew from Norway, marking a first orbital mission launched from continental Europe.
paragraphs: A rocket has reached orbit after launching from mainland Europe for the first time. The flight lifted off from Andoya Spaceport in northern Norway. It matters because Europe has been trying to build its own launch capacity as demand grows for small satellite missions and military access to space.

Europe has sent many satellites into space before, but usually from French Guiana in South America or on rockets launched elsewhere. This flight was different because the rocket left from continental Europe itself. The milestone comes as European governments and startups push for more local launch sites and less reliance on the United States and Russia.

Some key details are still unclear, including the payload carried, the exact orbit achieved, and how often launches from the site can follow. One successful mission does not create a full launch industry on its own. Operators still need repeat flights, safety approvals, customers, and enough rockets to make the route dependable.
stories.changes: It could give European satellite customers another place to launch small spacecraft closer to home.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Europe suddenly has cheap, routine launches or can match the biggest US rocket operators yet.

cover.title: Rocket reaches orbit after launch from Norway in European first
cover.standfirst: A small rocket launched from Andoya Spaceport in northern Norway and reached orbit, the first time an orbital mission has lifted off from mainland Europe. The flight is a step toward more European launch capacity. Officials and companies now need repeat missions, customers, and regulatory approval to make it routine.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: Make a brutal black paper cutout of Norway so the coastline itself reads instantly as a slim rocket in profile: the long body is the coast, the northern tip becomes the nose, and a small bite at Andoya is the ignition point. Set it against a flat hazard-orange ground with the rest of mainland Europe reduced to a low black mass at the bottom, quiet enough for cover lines; from Andoya, tear out a hard white exhaust plume and a few rough upward marker slashes so the Norway-shape is visibly pulling away from the continent, not just resembling a rocket.
art.note: Clean, public-works feel; cold blues, white snow, and one hot orange plume.
art.second_beat: First you see a rocket launch; a beat later you realise the rocket is Norway itself, turning continental geography into launch capability.

stories.headline: Ukraine spy chief says Russia can fund war until 2028
stories.dek: Kyiv says sanctions leaks, labor shortages and banking strain have not yet stopped Russia from sustaining its invasion.
paragraphs: Ukraine’s military intelligence chief said on September 7 that Russia still has enough resources to keep fighting through 2028. He said this now to warn Ukraine’s partners that sanctions are not cutting off key supplies fast enough, even as Russia’s economy shows clear signs of strain.

Oleh Ivashchenko said Russia faces a labor shortage, a growing budget deficit and pressure on its banks. But he said foreign-made electronic parts, machine tools and chemicals still reach Russia through front companies. He also said average daily Russian casualties run from 1,200 to 1,400, sometimes reaching 1,500.

These claims could not be independently verified from the interview alone, and it remains unclear how quickly tighter sanctions could reduce Russia’s war capacity. Ivashchenko also said more than 60% of Russians oppose the war, but it is not known whether that discontent can grow into organized protest.
stories.changes: For readers, this means the war is still likely to be long unless Russia’s supply lines and financing are hit harder.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Russia is economically healthy or certain to meet its war aims.

cover.title: Ukraine says Russia can keep funding the war until 2028
cover.standfirst: Ukraine’s military intelligence chief said on September 7 that Russia still has enough money, supplies and industrial inputs to sustain its war for three more years. He pointed to labor shortages, budget stress and bank pressure, but said sanctions leaks still let crucial parts and chemicals reach Russia.

art.label: Minimal mark
art.concept: A single small Matryoshka doll sits high and slightly off-centre in a wide pale field, leaving the lower third empty for type. Its body is open just enough to receive one oversized green microchip, shown mid-slide into the hollow cavity at a slight angle so it visibly should not fit but is still being forced in; keep everything else stripped away, with the doll unmistakably Russian by silhouette and pattern alone, no text or extra symbols.
art.note: Grave, stark, industrial; black, rust red and dirty gray.
art.second_beat: First read: Russia is still being supplied; second beat: the chip is illicit and unnatural—sanctions exist, but the part is still getting in.

stories.headline: AfD election surge in Saxony-Anhalt puts state power in reach
stories.dek: Exit polls put the far-right AfD first in the state, raising scrutiny of plans on schools, policing and migration.
paragraphs: Exit polls in Sunday’s Saxony-Anhalt state election put the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, in first place. That would make it the strongest party in the state and bring a far-right party closer to state power than at any time in postwar Germany. The result matters now because coalition talks and governing plans could follow.

The AfD is a nationalist, anti-immigration party that has grown from a protest force into a major player in German politics. In Saxony-Anhalt, reports have focused on ideas such as more segregated schooling and citizen watch groups. For readers outside Germany, states control many daily issues, including education, policing and local administration.

Exit polls are not final results, and first place does not mean the AfD will govern. Other parties may still try to block it from power through coalition deals. It is also unclear which parts of the party’s agenda could survive legal review, budget limits or resistance from schools, courts and civil servants.
stories.changes: If you live in Saxony-Anhalt, the election could affect schools, local security policy and how state institutions treat migrants and minorities.
stories.unchanged: Germany’s federal constitution, national government and immediate daily rules do not change overnight because one state party led the exit polls.

cover.title: AfD tops Saxony-Anhalt vote and nears state power
cover.standfirst: Exit polls from Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt put the far-right Alternative for Germany in first place. The result could shape coalition talks and bring its proposals on schools, migration and local security closer to government, though final results and alliances will decide whether it takes power.

art.label: Made object
art.concept: On a plain tabletop, place a small handmade clay school building from Saxony-Anhalt, seen three-quarter view, with its front door and ground-floor windows facing us. A thick surge of blue plasticine is actively bursting through the doorway and windows at the same moment, carrying just two unmistakable miniature state-life objects in the flow: a tiny school desk and a small clay police cap; keep the lower third largely clear and quiet for type, with the action concentrated in the middle and upper half.
art.note: Tense, civic mood; muted red, black and paper-cream palette.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a blue election ‘surge’; a beat later you see it is flooding directly into schools and policing — everyday state power, not abstract polling.

stories.headline: China injects $54 billion into state banks and insurers
stories.dek: Beijing widened a recapitalisation plan as weak profits, bad loans and slow growth weigh on major state-controlled financial groups.
paragraphs: China is putting about $54 billion into more state-controlled banks and insurers to strengthen their balance sheets and improve performance. The move comes as Beijing tries to support lending, shore up confidence and keep the financial system stable during a long property slump and weak economic growth.

China's biggest lenders and insurers are closely tied to the state and help carry out policy goals, from mortgage lending to support for local governments and developers. Many face pressure from thin margins, souring loans and weak demand for credit. Recapitalisation gives them fresh capital so they can absorb losses and keep operating.

It is not yet clear which institutions will receive how much, what conditions Beijing will attach, or whether new capital will be enough to fix deeper problems. The larger question is whether stronger bank balance sheets can revive borrowing and investment when households and businesses still feel cautious.
stories.changes: This may reduce the risk of sudden stress in China's financial system, which matters to savers, investors and companies that depend on Chinese growth.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean China's banking crisis is over, or that ordinary depositors in other countries need to do anything today.

cover.title: China puts $54 billion into state banks and insurers
cover.standfirst: Beijing has expanded a recapitalisation plan to more state-controlled financial groups, adding about $54 billion in fresh capital. The money is meant to strengthen bank and insurer balance sheets after weak profits, bad loans and a long property downturn. Details on recipients and conditions are still emerging.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: A single massive vertical chart bar dominates the page, but it is unmistakably also a syringe: broad rectangular barrel, plunger at the top, fine needle descending straight into the roofline of a low, generic Chinese state-bank facade stretched quietly across the bottom third. The bar/syringe is mid-injection, with one accent-colour column of liquid visibly travelling down inside it into the building, so the recapitalisation is literally the data point; keep everything else stripped away, with the bank signalled only by a restrained frontage and a couple of unmistakably Chinese institutional cues such as a roundel and formal colonnade, not logos or text.
art.note: Calm, precise mood; red, cream and charcoal palette.
art.second_beat: First you read a rising capital bar; a beat later you see it is a syringe injecting the bank, turning state recapitalisation itself into the chart.

stories.headline: Oil rises after Iran threatens new Strait of Hormuz exclusion zone
stories.dek: Brent crude neared $97 a barrel after Iran said it would tighten control near the world's most important oil shipping lane.
paragraphs: Oil prices rose Monday after a senior Iranian security official said Tehran would soon declare an exclusion zone outside the Strait of Hormuz. Traders reacted because the strait carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil, and any new restriction could cut supply further.

The warning came after days of military escalation. The United States said it disabled three Iranian oil tankers after Iran fired ballistic missiles at U.S. warships. Iran has kept the strait effectively constrained for months, and tanker traffic through the waterway has already fallen sharply.

It is still unclear where the exclusion zone would begin, which ships Iran would target, or how other navies would respond. Gulf states are split on strategy, South Korea has not decided on naval participation, and fuel prices could keep rising if shipping remains disrupted.
stories.changes: Drivers and businesses should expect higher fuel and shipping costs if oil traffic through the strait stays restricted.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all Gulf oil exports have stopped or that a full closure of the strait has been formally announced.

cover.title: Iran threat near Strait of Hormuz pushes oil prices higher
cover.standfirst: Brent crude rose to $96.95 a barrel after Iran said it would announce an exclusion zone outside the Strait of Hormuz. The threat follows U.S. strikes on three Iranian tankers, and tanker traffic through the key oil route has already dropped sharply.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint a huge loaded supertanker jammed crosswise inside the narrow throat of a petrol-pump nozzle, the nozzle enlarged just enough to read instantly but still absurdly tight around the hull. Behind the ship, crude-dark sea and oil mass up under the Iranian headland, while beyond the nozzle tip only a thin trickle escapes into open water; keep Oman and Iran as two blunt coast shapes so the choke point unmistakably reads as Hormuz, and leave the lower third as mostly flat dark water and reflection for type.
art.note: Tense and spare, with navy, sand, and a hard red accent.
art.second_beat: First you see a tanker stuck in a nozzle; a beat later you realise the device meant to dispense oil has become the Strait’s choke point stopping it.
